# The data

`L09_workshops.csv` records one month of activity for the 320 artisan workshops
that belong to a regional consortium. Every statement made below describes these
320 workshops exactly: nothing is inferred about workshops outside the file.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `workshop_id` | Identifier of the workshop |
| `province_code` | Province of registration, coded 1 to 4 |
| `craft` | Craft practised: Ceramics, Leather, Woodwork, Textiles |
| `qualification` | Level held by the head of the workshop: Apprentice, Craftsman, Master |
| `years_active` | Completed years the workshop has been active |
| `price_per_piece` | List price of a piece, averaged over the workshop's catalogue, in euros |
| `pieces_sold` | Pieces sold during the month |
| `quality_score` | Consortium quality score for the month, from 1 to 5 |
| `monthly_revenue` | Total takings for the month, in euros: sales net of discounts, plus commissions, courses and repairs |
| `exports` | Whether the workshop sold abroad during the month |

Because of discounts on one side and non-sales income on the other,
`monthly_revenue` is not the product of `price_per_piece` and `pieces_sold`.

Four exercises. Fill the chunks; the questions that close each one are there for
you to check your own understanding, and are not handed in.

```{r import}
workshops <- read.csv("L09_workshops.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

str(workshops)
```

---

# Exercise 1 — Measurement scales, position and shape

1. Run `summary()` on the data frame and identify the column with missing values
   and how many there are.
2. Compute `mean(workshops$province_code)`. Then convert `qualification` into an
   **ordered** factor with its levels in the correct order and check it with
   `table()`.
3. Compute mean, median and the five-number summary of `monthly_revenue`, and the
   sample skewness $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i z_i^3$, where $z_i$ is the standardized
   variable computed with `mean()` and `sd()`.
4. Recompute mean and median after removing the largest workshop, with
   `workshops$monthly_revenue[-which.max(workshops$monthly_revenue)]`, and compare
   the two displacements.

```{r ex1}
summary(workshops)

# Report only columns that contain missing observations.
missing_counts <- colSums(is.na(workshops))
print(missing_counts[missing_counts > 0])
stopifnot(nrow(workshops) == 320, ncol(workshops) == 10,
          missing_counts["quality_score"] == 11)

mean(workshops$province_code)
workshops$qualification <- factor(
  workshops$qualification,
  levels = c("Apprentice", "Craftsman", "Master"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
levels(workshops$qualification)
is.ordered(workshops$qualification)
table(workshops$qualification)

revenue <- workshops$monthly_revenue
revenue_mean <- mean(revenue)
revenue_median <- median(revenue)
z <- (revenue - mean(revenue)) / sd(revenue)
revenue_skewness <- mean(z^3)

print(c(Mean_EUR = revenue_mean, Median_EUR = revenue_median,
        Sample_skewness = revenue_skewness))
print(setNames(fivenum(revenue),
               c("Minimum", "Lower hinge", "Median", "Upper hinge", "Maximum")))

# This expression removes exactly one observation; keep the full dataset intact.
revenue_without_largest <-
  workshops$monthly_revenue[-which.max(workshops$monthly_revenue)]
stopifnot(length(revenue_without_largest) == length(revenue) - 1)
mean_without_largest <- mean(revenue_without_largest)
median_without_largest <- median(revenue_without_largest)

print(data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean (EUR)", "Median (EUR)"),
  Full_data = c(revenue_mean, revenue_median),
  Largest_removed = c(mean_without_largest, median_without_largest),
  Change_removed_minus_full = c(mean_without_largest - revenue_mean,
                               median_without_largest - revenue_median)
))

```

> **(a)** Classify `province_code`, `qualification`, `years_active` and
> `monthly_revenue` on the four measurement scales, and state for each the highest
> admissible measure of centre. Why did R return a number for the mean of
> `province_code`?
> **(b)** What does the sign of the skewness, together with the relative position
> of mean and median, say about the distribution of the revenue?
> **(c)** Which of the two summaries moved when the largest workshop was removed,
> and which property accounts for it?

# Exercise 2 — Variability and concentration

1. Compute the standard deviation and the IQR of `monthly_revenue`, and the
   coefficient of variation $s/\bar{x}$ of `monthly_revenue`, `pieces_sold` and
   `price_per_piece`.
2. For $k = 1.5, 2, 3$, compute the observed proportion of values within $k$
   standard deviations of the mean and compare it with the Bienaymé–Chebyshev
   bound $1 - 1/k^2$.
3. Draw the Lorenz curve of `monthly_revenue` and compute the Gini index as twice
   the area between the diagonal and the curve:

```r
x <- sort(workshops$monthly_revenue)
p <- (0:length(x)) / length(x)          # cumulative share of workshops
q <- c(0, cumsum(x)) / sum(x)           # cumulative share of total revenue
plot(p, q, type = "l"); abline(0, 1, lty = 2)

area <- sum(diff(p) * (head(q, -1) + tail(q, -1)) / 2)
1 - 2 * area
```

   Read off the share of the total taken by the poorer half and by the top decile.

4. Draw the histogram of `monthly_revenue` with `breaks = 10` and with
   `breaks = 60`. Assign each call to an object and report, for both, the number
   of classes actually drawn, `length(h$counts)`, and their width,
   `diff(h$breaks)[1]`.

```{r ex2, fig.height=4}
revenue <- workshops$monthly_revenue
print(c(SD_EUR = sd(revenue), IQR_EUR = IQR(revenue)))

cv_variables <- c("monthly_revenue", "pieces_sold", "price_per_piece")
cv <- sapply(workshops[cv_variables], function(x) sd(x) / mean(x))
print(data.frame(Variable = names(cv), CV = unname(cv)))

k <- c(1.5, 2, 3)
observed_proportion <- sapply(k, function(ki) {
  mean(abs(revenue - mean(revenue)) <= ki * sd(revenue))
})
chebyshev_bound <- 1 - 1 / k^2
print(data.frame(
  k = k,
  Observed_proportion = observed_proportion,
  Chebyshev_lower_bound = chebyshev_bound,
  Observed_minus_bound = observed_proportion - chebyshev_bound
))

x <- sort(workshops$monthly_revenue)
p <- (0:length(x)) / length(x)
q <- c(0, cumsum(x)) / sum(x)
# A square plotting region keeps both cumulative-share axes between 0 and 1.
old_pty <- par("pty")
par(pty = "s")
plot(p, q, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#245E85", asp = 1,
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     main = "Lorenz curve of monthly revenue",
     xlab = "Cumulative share of workshops",
     ylab = "Cumulative share of total revenue")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("topleft", c("Monthly revenue", "Equal-revenue diagonal"),
       col = c("#245E85", "grey50"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(pty = old_pty)

# Trapezoids give the area under the empirical Lorenz curve.
area <- sum(diff(p) * (head(q, -1) + tail(q, -1)) / 2)
gini <- 1 - 2 * area
print(c(Lorenz_area = area, Gini_index = gini))

# For 320 workshops, these groups contain exactly 160 and 32 observations.
bottom_n <- length(x) / 2
top_n <- length(x) / 10
bottom50_share <- sum(head(x, bottom_n)) / sum(x)
top10_share <- sum(tail(x, top_n)) / sum(x)
print(data.frame(
  Group = c("Bottom 50%", "Top 10%"),
  Workshops = c(bottom_n, top_n),
  Revenue_share = c(bottom50_share, top10_share),
  Revenue_percent = 100 * c(bottom50_share, top10_share)
))

h10 <- hist(revenue, breaks = 10, col = "#9DBDD2", border = "white",
            main = "Monthly revenue: breaks = 10",
            xlab = "Monthly revenue (EUR)", ylab = "Number of workshops")
h60 <- hist(revenue, breaks = 60, col = "#9DBDD2", border = "white",
            main = "Monthly revenue: breaks = 60",
            xlab = "Monthly revenue (EUR)", ylab = "Number of workshops")
print(data.frame(
  Requested_breaks = c(10, 60),
  Actual_bins = c(length(h10$counts), length(h60$counts)),
  Bin_width_EUR = c(diff(h10$breaks)[1], diff(h60$breaks)[1])
))

```

> **(a)** Why can the standard deviations of `monthly_revenue` and `pieces_sold`
> not be compared directly, and what does the coefficient of variation change?
> **(b)** The observed proportions exceed the Chebyshev bounds by a wide margin.
> Is that a defect of the inequality, of the data, or of neither?
> **(c)** What does the Gini index measure that the standard deviation does not?
> Which of the two histograms would you use, and why is the choice not neutral?

# Exercise 3 — Association between two categorical variables

1. Build the contingency table of `qualification` by `craft` and the conditional
   distribution of `qualification` within each craft
   (`prop.table(tab, margin = 2)`).
2. Compute the chi-square statistic with `chisq.test()` and Cramér's V,
   $V = \sqrt{\chi^2 / (n \cdot (\min(r,c) - 1))}$.
3. Measure the dependence in mean of `price_per_piece` on `qualification` through
   eta-squared, the ratio of the between-group deviance to the total deviance, and
   draw the box-plots of `price_per_piece` by `qualification`:

```r
grand_mean  <- mean(workshops$price_per_piece)
group_means <- tapply(workshops$price_per_piece, workshops$qualification, mean)
group_n     <- table(workshops$qualification)

sum(group_n * (group_means - grand_mean)^2) /
  sum((workshops$price_per_piece - grand_mean)^2)
```

```{r ex3, fig.height=4}
tab <- table(workshops$qualification, workshops$craft)
print(tab)
conditional <- prop.table(tab, margin = 2)
print(conditional)

# The supplied setup hides warnings, so capture and report any test warning.
chi_warnings <- character(0)
chi <- withCallingHandlers(
  chisq.test(tab),
  warning = function(w) {
    chi_warnings <<- c(chi_warnings, conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
print(chi)
n <- sum(tab)
r <- nrow(tab)
c <- ncol(tab)
cramers_v <- sqrt(unname(chi$statistic) / (n * (min(r, c) - 1)))
print(c(Cramers_V = cramers_v))

cat("Expected counts:\n")
print(chi$expected)
print(c(Minimum_expected = min(chi$expected),
        Cells_below_5 = sum(chi$expected < 5),
        Cells_below_1 = sum(chi$expected < 1)))
cat("All expected counts are at least 5:", all(chi$expected >= 5), "\n")
cat("Chi-square warnings:",
    if (length(chi_warnings)) paste(chi_warnings, collapse = "; ") else "none",
    "\n")
cat("Each workshop has one record; independence between workshops cannot",
    "be established from the contingency table alone.\n")

grand_mean <- mean(workshops$price_per_piece)
group_means <- tapply(workshops$price_per_piece, workshops$qualification, mean)
group_n <- table(workshops$qualification)
between_deviance <- sum(group_n * (group_means - grand_mean)^2)
total_deviance <- sum((workshops$price_per_piece - grand_mean)^2)
eta_squared <- between_deviance / total_deviance
print(c(Between_group_deviance = between_deviance,
        Total_deviance = total_deviance, Eta_squared = eta_squared))

boxplot(price_per_piece ~ qualification, data = workshops,
        main = "Price per piece by qualification",
        xlab = "Qualification (ordered)", ylab = "Price per piece (EUR)",
        col = c("#C9DBE8", "#91B5CD", "#5689AE"))

```

> **(a)** Why is a comparison of the raw counts not evidence of association, and
> which comparison is? What would independence in distribution look like in the
> table of conditional distributions?
> **(b)** Which of $\chi^2$ and $V$ would be roughly unchanged if the consortium
> had ten times as many workshops with the same percentage profile, and why?
> **(c)** Interpret the value of eta-squared in one sentence.

# Exercise 4 — Association between two quantitative variables

1. Compute the Pearson and the Spearman correlation matrices for `years_active`,
   `price_per_piece`, `pieces_sold`, `quality_score` and `monthly_revenue`
   (`use = "complete.obs"`), and subtract the first from the second.
2. Plot `quality_score` against `pieces_sold` and compute the Pearson correlation
   of the pair.

```{r ex4, fig.height=4}
variables <- c("years_active", "price_per_piece", "pieces_sold",
               "quality_score", "monthly_revenue")
quantitative <- workshops[variables]
cat("Complete observations for both matrices:",
    sum(complete.cases(quantitative)), "of", nrow(workshops), "\n")

pearson <- cor(quantitative, method = "pearson", use = "complete.obs")
spearman <- cor(quantitative, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
correlation_difference <- spearman - pearson
cat("Pearson correlation matrix:\n")
print(pearson, digits = 4)
cat("Spearman correlation matrix:\n")
print(spearman, digits = 4)
cat("Difference: Spearman minus Pearson:\n")
print(correlation_difference, digits = 4)

# Remove incomplete pairs together so the two vectors remain aligned.
pair <- workshops[complete.cases(workshops[c("quality_score", "pieces_sold")]),
                  c("quality_score", "pieces_sold")]
pair_r <- cor(pair$pieces_sold, pair$quality_score, method = "pearson")
print(c(Complete_pairs = nrow(pair), Pearson_r = pair_r))
plot(pair$pieces_sold, pair$quality_score,
     pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#245E85", alpha.f = 0.6),
     main = sprintf("Quality score against pieces sold\nPearson r = %.4f; n = %d",
                    pair_r, nrow(pair)),
     xlab = "Pieces sold during the month",
     ylab = "Consortium quality score (1 to 5)")

```

> **(a)** Which variable appears in the two largest Spearman–Pearson gaps, and
> what does a positive gap indicate about the form of the relationship?
> **(b)** The correlation between `quality_score` and `pieces_sold` is close to
> zero. Does it follow that the two variables are unrelated?
